proof_nl:
Let e_i be the i-th standard basis vector of length m (so e_i has a 1 in position i and 0 elsewhere). For a sign string t, define c_t(i)=Total(T_t(e_i)). Since U, D, and Total are linear, T_t is linear, hence for every x=(x_1,...,x_m),
Total(T_t(x))=sum_{i=1}^m c_t(i)x_i.
So it is enough to understand the coefficients c_t(i).

For t=(t_1,...,t_r) and indices i,j, call a sequence p_0,p_1,...,p_r an admissible t-chain from i to j if p_0=i, p_r=j, 1<=p_k<=m+k for each k, and for each k:
- if t_k=+1, then p_{k-1}<p_k;
- if t_k=-1, then p_{k-1}>=p_k.
I claim that T_t(e_i)_j is exactly the number of admissible t-chains from i to j.

This is proved by induction on r. For r=1, if t=(+1), then U(e_i)_j=1 exactly when i<j and 0 otherwise, so it counts one-step admissible chains. If t=(-1), then D(e_i)_j=1 exactly when i>=j and 0 otherwise, so it again counts one-step admissible chains.

For the induction step, suppose the claim is true for a sign string t of length r, and let t' be obtained by appending one more sign. If the new sign is +1, then for each j,
T_{t'}(e_i)_j=U(T_t(e_i))_j=sum_{h=1}^{j-1} T_t(e_i)_h.
By the induction hypothesis, this counts exactly the admissible t-chains from i to h, summed over all h<j; that is exactly the number of admissible t'-chains from i to j. If the new sign is -1, then similarly
T_{t'}(e_i)_j=D(T_t(e_i))_j=sum_{h=j}^{m+r} T_t(e_i)_h,
which counts exactly the admissible t'-chains from i to j. Thus the claim holds for all r.

Therefore c_t(i)=Total(T_t(e_i)) is the number of admissible t-chains starting at i, with arbitrary endpoint.

Now let a_i=c_{Alt_r^+}(i). Because the first sign of Alt_r^+ is +1, every admissible Alt_r^+-chain starting at i+1 is also admissible starting at i: indeed the only condition involving the start is p_0<p_1, and i+1<p_1 implies i<p_1. Hence a_i>=a_{i+1}.

This inclusion is strict for every i<m. Consider the chain defined by
p_0=i,
p_1=i+1,
and for k>=2,
p_k=1 if k is even, and p_k=m+k if k is odd.
This satisfies the alternating conditions +,-,+,-,..., so it is an admissible Alt_r^+-chain starting at i. But it is not admissible starting at i+1, because its first step would require i+1<p_1=i+1, which is false. Therefore
a_1>a_2>...>a_m.

Next let b_i=c_{Alt_r^-}(i). I claim that b_i=a_{m+1-i}. Take any admissible Alt_r^+-chain p_0=i,p_1,...,p_r and define
q_k=m+k+1-p_k  for 0<=k<=r.
Then q_0=m+1-i and 1<=q_k<=m+k for every k. Also, Alt_r^- is obtained from Alt_r^+ by flipping every sign, and the inequalities transform correctly:
- if the k-th sign of Alt_r^+ is +1, then p_{k-1}<p_k, so
  q_{k-1}-q_k=(m+k-p_{k-1})-(m+k+1-p_k)=p_k-p_{k-1}-1>=0,
  hence q_{k-1}>=q_k;
- if the k-th sign of Alt_r^+ is -1, then p_{k-1}>=p_k, so
  q_{k-1}-q_k=p_k-p_{k-1}-1<=-1,
  hence q_{k-1}<q_k.
So q is an admissible Alt_r^--chain starting at m+1-i. The same transformation is its own inverse, so this is a bijection. Hence b_i=a_{m+1-i}.

Now define
F_+(x)=Total(T_{Alt_r^+}(x)),
F_-(x)=Total(T_{Alt_r^-}(x)).
By linearity and the identities above,
F_+(x)=sum_{i=1}^m a_i x_i,
F_-(x)=sum_{i=1}^m a_{m+1-i} x_i.
Therefore
F_+(x)-F_-(x)=sum_{i=1}^m (a_i-a_{m+1-i})x_i.
Pairing the terms with indices i and m+1-i gives
F_+(x)-F_-(x)=sum_{i=1}^{floor(m/2)} (a_i-a_{m+1-i})(x_i-x_{m+1-i}).
Because a_1>a_2>...>a_m, each coefficient a_i-a_{m+1-i} in this sum is positive.

If x is nonnegative and nonincreasing, then x_i>=x_{m+1-i} for every i<=floor(m/2). Hence every term in the last sum is >=0, so F_+(x)>=F_-(x). If x is nonconstant, then x_1>x_m, and since a_1>a_m, the term with i=1 is >0; therefore F_+(x)>F_-(x).

If x is nonnegative and nondecreasing, then x_i<=x_{m+1-i} for every i<=floor(m/2). Hence every term in the last sum is <=0, so F_+(x)<=F_-(x), i.e. F_-(x)>=F_+(x). If x is nonconstant, then x_1<x_m, so the term with i=1 is <0; therefore F_+(x)<F_-(x).

This is exactly the stated lemma.
solver_summary: Expand the total as a linear combination of the coordinates of x using basis vectors. For Alt_r^+, the coefficient of x_i counts alternating index-chains starting at i; this count is strictly decreasing in i because the first step is a strict ascent. Complementing each intermediate index gives a bijection showing that the Alt_r^- coefficients are the reverse of the Alt_r^+ coefficients. Pairing symmetric indices then yields the required sign of the difference for monotone x, with strictness for nonconstant x.
vetter_reason: The proof is complete and internally coherent. It correctly expresses Total∘T_t as a linear functional on x, identifies the coefficients via an induction that counts admissible chains, proves strict monotonicity of the coefficient sequence for Alt_r^+ by an inclusion-plus-witness argument, derives the Alt_r^- coefficients by an explicit involutive reflection bijection, and then finishes by pairing symmetric indices to compare the two totals for monotone x. The strictness arguments for nonconstant weakly monotone x are also valid. No forbidden or undeclared dependencies are used.
